Cloud-Native Principles: Designing for elasticity, failure & change

slides.title: Three Core Principles
slides.lead: Cloud-native design means building an application assuming its servers, network paths and traffic levels will all change constantly, rather than bolting resilience on after an outage

points.text: Elasticity: capacity expands and shrinks automatically with real demand
Failure tolerance: the system keeps serving when a component dies
Ease of change: new code and configuration roll out without downtime

slides.notes: "Frame cloud-native as a mindset, not a tool: design decisions made upfront because failure is routine, not exceptional. Point to the three boxes as the roadmap for this section. Interview angle: cloud-native versus merely 'lifted-and-shifted' legacy apps."

slides.label: Analogy: automatic traffic signal
slides.title: Three Core Principles
slides.notes: TR analogy: An automatic traffic signal adjusts its timing based on traffic flow, handling busy and quiet periods efficiently: just as cloud-native applications adjust resources based on demand and are designed to handle failures. "Frame cloud-native as a mindset, not a tool: design decisions made upfront because failure is routine, not exceptional. Point to the three boxes as the roadmap for this section. Interview angle: cloud-native versus merely 'lifted-and-shifted' legacy apps."

slides.title: Scaling As Default
slides.lead: Designing for elasticity means building components that scale independently and externalizing state where possible, so capacity can be added by launching more instances rather than resizing one

points.text: Auto Scaling Groups attach new instances to the load balancer's target group
Reactive scaling adds capacity when a CloudWatch alarm threshold is breached
Predictive scaling forecasts demand from historical traffic patterns in advance

slides.notes: "Emphasise that elasticity is a design choice, not just an AWS feature: the application must tolerate instances appearing and disappearing. Point to the Auto Scaling Groups console as where this is configured. Exam hook: why a stateful component cannot scale elastically without extra work."

slides.title: Scaling As Default

points.text: Stateless components scale out freely
Stateful components are harder to scale because they must manage shared or persistent state

note.text: For variable demand, right-sized elastic fleets usually cost less than one large fixed server, since idle capacity is released when demand drops

slides.notes: "Emphasise that elasticity is a design choice, not just an AWS feature: the application must tolerate instances appearing and disappearing. Point to the Auto Scaling Groups console as where this is configured. Exam hook: why a stateful component cannot scale elastically without extra work."

slides.title: Assume It Breaks
slides.lead: Where the single-point-of-failure problem is solved by adding backend servers, cloud-native design goes further: it assumes any single component, availability zone, or dependency can fail without warning, and contains the damage

points.text: Multi-AZ deployment runs instances in separate Availability Zones
Each made of one or more isolated data centers, so one zone failing does not stop the application
Bulkhead isolation confines one service's failure from spreading system-wide

slides.notes: "Explain that failure tolerance means designing the blast radius small, not just adding a spare server. Point to the Fault Injection Service console as where teams deliberately rehearse failure. Interview hook: ask the difference between redundancy and fault isolation."

slides.title: Assume It Breaks

points.text: Blast radius: how much of the system one failure can reach
AWS Fault Injection Service deliberately breaks components to test recovery

slides.notes: "Explain that failure tolerance means designing the blast radius small, not just adding a spare server. Point to the Fault Injection Service console as where teams deliberately rehearse failure. Interview hook: ask the difference between redundancy and fault isolation."

slides.title: Immutable Infrastructure
slides.lead: Cloud-native systems expect frequent deployment, so they replace running instances with a new machine image rather than editing a live server, keeping every environment reproducible

points.text: Immutable infrastructure replaces running instances with newly built and tested ones instead of modifying them in place
Infrastructure as Code templates recreate identical environments on demand
Loosely coupled services deploy independently without a full-system restart

note.text: Together, elasticity, failure tolerance and ease of change shape how configuration, processes and logging are structured next

slides.notes: "Stress that immutability removes configuration drift, since no server is ever hand-edited after launch. Point to how an updated machine image replaces, rather than patches, a fleet. Exam hook: why immutable infrastructure pairs naturally with Infrastructure as Code."
The Twelve-Factor App: Config & backing services; processes & disposability; logs as event streams

slides.title: A Portability Checklist
slides.lead: Apps once broke when moved between environments. The Twelve-Factor App, published by Heroku engineers in 2011, is a 12-rule checklist for portable, cloud-ready software

points.text: The 12 factors cover code, dependencies, config, services, builds, processes, ports, scaling, shutdown, parity, logs and admin tasks
Five matter most for cloud-native: config, backing services, processes, disposability and logs

slides.notes: "Open by noting cloud apps once broke when moved between environments, which is the gap this methodology closes. Mention Heroku's 2011 origin as an interview-relevant fact. Point out that only three of the twelve factors are covered in this session."

slides.title: A Portability Checklist

points.text: Each factor fixes one operational failure, not a style choice
Widely followed when building apps for platforms
Such as Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk and Kubernetes

slides.notes: "Open by noting cloud apps once broke when moved between environments, which is the gap this methodology closes. Mention Heroku's 2011 origin as an interview-relevant fact. Point out that only three of the twelve factors are covered in this session."

slides.label: Analogy: travel checklist
slides.title: A Portability Checklist
slides.notes: TR analogy: A travel checklist helps people prepare for different trips by covering essentials like tickets, documents, luggage and transport. The Twelve-Factor App works similarly by providing a common set of principles for building and running applications reliably across different environments. "Open by noting cloud apps once broke when moved between environments, which is the gap this methodology closes. Mention Heroku's 2011 origin as an interview-relevant fact. Point out that only three of the twelve factors are covered in this session."

slides.title: Decoupling App From Env
slides.lead: The config factor keeps every environment-specific value outside the code, so one build runs unchanged anywhere. A backing service is any resource the application consumes over the network, attached only through that config

points.text: Config: database URLs and feature flags live in environment variables
API keys and passwords come from a secret store
Same codebase deploys to dev, staging and production by changing only config

slides.notes: "Stress that config covers every environment value, including but not limited to secrets. Use the RDS and SQS endpoint example to show the same build moving across environments. Ask: why can the same image run unchanged in staging and production?"

slides.title: Decoupling App From Env

points.text: Backing service: a network-consumed resource: database, queue, cache or SMTP server
Swapping a backing service of the same type, such as a local MySQL database for Amazon RDS
Needs only a config change, not a code change
AWS example: RDS endpoint and SQS queue URL passed as environment variables

slides.notes: "Stress that config covers every environment value, including but not limited to secrets. Use the RDS and SQS endpoint example to show the same build moving across environments. Ask: why can the same image run unchanged in staging and production?"

slides.title: Stateless By Design
slides.lead: Where config makes an application portable, disposability makes it elastic: each process instance must start, work and terminate without any special handling or memory of its own

points.text: Process: application runs as stateless, share-nothing processes
Session state lives in backing services, never in process memory

slides.notes: "Tie statelessness to disposability: a process with no memory of its own loses nothing when it is killed. Give the example of a container task starting in seconds to meet an autoscaling trigger. Interview hook: ask what happens to an in-flight request when an instance is scaled in."

slides.title: Stateless By Design

points.text: Disposability: processes start within a few seconds and shut down on signal
Graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests before the process exits
Fast startup lets autoscaling add capacity quickly, keeping idle cost low

slides.notes: "Tie statelessness to disposability: a process with no memory of its own loses nothing when it is killed. Give the example of a container task starting in seconds to meet an autoscaling trigger. Interview hook: ask what happens to an in-flight request when an instance is scaled in."

slides.title: No Local Log Files
slides.lead: A disposable process can't rely on a local log file, which disappears with it. Twelve-factor treats logs as a time-ordered event stream written to standard output

points.text: Application writes log events to standard output instead of managing local log files
Container runtime or host platform captures the stream in real time
A log router aggregates streams off the host for central storage

slides.notes: "Explain why writing to a local log file fails once the container disposes of itself. Point to CloudWatch Logs as the real AWS location collecting these streams. Interview hook: ask why twelve-factor forbids an application from managing its own log files."

slides.title: No Local Log Files

points.text: Centralised storage keeps logs accessible after the process is destroyed
AWS location: container logs land in Amazon CloudWatch Logs log groups

slides.notes: "Explain why writing to a local log file fails once the container disposes of itself. Point to CloudWatch Logs as the real AWS location collecting these streams. Interview hook: ask why twelve-factor forbids an application from managing its own log files."

slides.title: Bridge To Architecture
slides.lead: A disposable, config-driven process is the basic unit a cloud platform scales; how many such units make up one system, and how they communicate, decides the application's architecture

points.text: Twelve-factor principles make horizontal scaling and resilience patterns easier to apply
Stateless, disposable processes can be replaced safely during scaling or failure
The same discipline applies whether the system is one service or many

slides.notes: "Close by stating that twelve-factor compliance is what lets a platform scale and replace instances automatically. Note that this discipline holds whether the system is one service or many. Interview hook: ask why disposability matters for autoscaling cost."
Monolith vs Microservices: Trade-offs; service boundaries; inter-service communication

slides.title: Two Architecture Styles
slides.lead: A monolith bundles every feature into one codebase and deployment unit. Microservices split that into many independent services, each owning one business capability

points.text: Monolith: tightly coupled modules deployed together, usually sharing one database
Microservices: each service keeps its own datastore and API
Companies split monoliths into microservices mainly to scale parts independently

slides.notes: "Explain monolith as one big program and microservices as the same features split into independent small programs, using the kitchen-versus-food-court picture. Interviewers ask why companies migrate to microservices: independent scaling is the answer."

slides.label: Analogy: school office
slides.title: Two Architecture Styles
slides.notes: TR analogy: A single school office manages admissions, fees and exams together, so a rush in admissions slows everything. Separate offices handle each function independently, so the fees office can add staff during fee week without changing the others. This is similar to monolithic and microservices architectures. "Explain monolith as one big program and microservices as the same features split into independent small programs, using the kitchen-versus-food-court picture. Interviewers ask why companies migrate to microservices: independent scaling is the answer."

slides.title: Comparing The Costs
slides.lead: Splitting an application into services shifts complexity from code into the network. The right choice depends on team size, release frequency and how failures should be contained

cells: One unit redeployed for any change
One crash can take down everything
A failing service can be isolated from the rest

cells.text: Elastic Beanstalk or a single EC2 fleet
Separate services on ECS or EKS

note.text: Scaling only the busy service costs less than scaling an entire monolith to handle one bottleneck

slides.notes: "Walk through each row, stressing that microservices trade simplicity for independent scaling and fault containment. Point to the AWS row to ground this in ECS and EKS. Ask when a monolith is still correct: low traffic, small team."

slides.title: Where To Split
slides.lead: Splitting a monolith helps only when each service maps to one business capability; a boundary drawn through the wrong seam forces services to call each other constantly

points.text: Boundary follows a business capability: orders, payments, inventory separately
Each service owns its data; other services reach it through the service's API, never its tables
High cohesion inside a service, loose coupling across services
This bounded-context grouping comes from domain-driven design practice

slides.notes: "Stress that boundaries follow business capabilities, not technical layers like all-database-code, using orders split from payments as the example. This is the bounded-context idea from domain-driven design, often asked as how to size a microservice."

slides.title: Sync Vs Async Calls
slides.lead: Once services run as separate processes across a network, they must call each other directly or through an intermediary: unlike modules in a single codebase, which call each other in the same process

points.text: Synchronous: REST or gRPC call, caller waits for the response
Asynchronous: a message queue or event bus decouples sender and receiver

slides.notes: "Explain synchronous calls as a phone call where the caller waits, asynchronous as leaving a message read later. Point to API Gateway and SQS as the concrete AWS services for each pattern. Ask when to choose async over sync: decoupling and resilience to downstream failures."

slides.title: Sync Vs Async Calls

points.text: API gateway gives clients one entry point to many services
AWS maps these to API Gateway and SQS or SNS

note.text: These communication choices shape how a container-orchestration platform routes traffic between running service instances

slides.notes: "Explain synchronous calls as a phone call where the caller waits, asynchronous as leaving a message read later. Point to API Gateway and SQS as the concrete AWS services for each pattern. Ask when to choose async over sync: decoupling and resilience to downstream failures."
Statelessness: Stateless vs stateful workloads; externalizing state

slides.title: Two Workload Types
slides.lead: Cloud-native design keeps requests independent so an elastic fleet can add or remove instances without losing user data. A stateless workload keeps no client data between calls; a stateful one must remember past interactions

points.text: Stateless examples: web front ends, API tiers, Lambda functions
Stateful examples: relational databases, message queues, legacy session stores

slides.notes: "Stress that statelessness is an architecture-level design choice, not only something inside one function. Ask: why can a stateless instance be killed and replaced freely while a database node cannot? Interviewers often probe this distinction when asking how a system scales."

slides.title: Two Workload Types

points.text: Elasticity assumes any healthy stateless instance can serve any request
So instances are easy to replace
Stateful components need identity or replication to survive restarts

slides.notes: "Stress that statelessness is an architecture-level design choice, not only something inside one function. Ask: why can a stateless instance be killed and replaced freely while a database node cannot? Interviewers often probe this distinction when asking how a system scales."

slides.label: Analogy: hotel receptionists
slides.title: Two Workload Types
slides.notes: TR analogy: In one hotel, guest details are stored in a central system, so any receptionist can assist them (stateless). In another, each receptionist remembers guest details personally, so guests must return to the same receptionist (stateful). "Stress that statelessness is an architecture-level design choice, not only something inside one function. Ask: why can a stateless instance be killed and replaced freely while a database node cannot? Interviewers often probe this distinction when asking how a system scales."

slides.title: Where State Lives
slides.lead: Because instances disappear on scale-in or failure, anything that must outlive a single request moves out of the compute tier into a dedicated backing service

points.text: Session and cache data: externalized to a shared cache such as Amazon ElastiCache
Durable records: externalized to a managed database such as DynamoDB or RDS
Uploaded files and binaries: externalized to object storage such as Amazon S3
Configuration and secrets: pulled from a config store, not baked into the image

slides.notes: "Point out this is the backing-services idea applied specifically to state rather than configuration. Ask: if a cache node fails, does the stateless web tier lose any data? Mention DynamoDB and ElastiCache as the typical real-world choices."

slides.title: Session Survives Swap
slides.lead: An auto-scaling group terminates an unhealthy instance mid-session; because the session itself was externalized, the next request succeeds without the user noticing

points.text: Instance `i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890` on `10.0.1.15`
Fails a health check on port `8080`
Auto Scaling launches replacement instance `i-0f9e8d7c6b5a43210` within a few minutes

slides.notes: "Walk through the timeline as a sequence, stressing that the cache: not either instance: is the source of truth. Ask: what breaks here if the session lived only in the first instance's local memory? This is a classic interview probe on designing for failure."

slides.title: Session Survives Swap

points.text: Session key `sess_7f3a2b` stays in ElastiCache with a 30-minute TTL
New instance reads the same session key from the shared cache
The user stays logged in through the swap

slides.notes: "Walk through the timeline as a sequence, stressing that the cache: not either instance: is the source of truth. Ask: what breaks here if the session lived only in the first instance's local memory? This is a classic interview probe on designing for failure."

slides.title: Trade-offs Compared
slides.lead: Externalizing state is not free: it adds a network hop and a dependency on the backing service's own availability, so some workloads are stateful by necessity
slides.notes: "Emphasise that stateful is not a design flaw: a database genuinely needs persistent identity. Ask: why can a stateless web tier scale with a simple policy while a database cannot scale the same way? This distinction anchors the scaling and resilience patterns coming up."
Scalability & Resilience Patterns: Horizontal scaling, caching & queues; retries, timeouts, circuit breakers & graceful degradation

slides.title: Handling Failure At Scale
slides.lead: Distributed cloud systems fail in parts routinely; resilience patterns keep the rest of the system working when one piece does not

points.text: Horizontal scaling: adding more instances to share growing load
Caching and queues: reduce load and absorb traffic bursts

slides.notes: "Frame this as the toolbox for staying available when parts fail; name all five, detail comes on later slides. Exam hook: list all five patterns in one line."

slides.title: Handling Failure At Scale

points.text: Retries and timeouts: bound the wait and retry with backoff
To recover from brief failures
Circuit breakers: stop calls to a failing service quickly
Graceful degradation: serve a reduced response instead of none

slides.notes: "Frame this as the toolbox for staying available when parts fail; name all five, detail comes on later slides. Exam hook: list all five patterns in one line."

slides.title: Capacity And Resilience
slides.lead: Adding more identical instances behind a load balancer spreads load and also removes any single instance as a point of failure

points.text: Replaces one large server with many smaller, interchangeable instances
A failing instance is swapped out without disrupting other requests
Needs externalized state, since any instance may handle any request

slides.notes: "Point out that horizontal scaling doubles as a resilience tool, not just a capacity one, and depends on statelessness. Exam hook: why can horizontal scaling only work with stateless services?"

slides.title: Capacity And Resilience

points.text: AWS: Auto Scaling Groups add instances behind a load balancer
Cost: scaling out adds instance-hour cost but buys fault isolation

slides.notes: "Point out that horizontal scaling doubles as a resilience tool, not just a capacity one, and depends on statelessness. Exam hook: why can horizontal scaling only work with stateless services?"

slides.title: Absorbing Load Spikes
slides.lead: Caching keeps popular data close by so repeat reads skip the slow path; a queue holds work until a consumer is ready

points.text: Cache-aside: application checks cache first, falls back to the database
Queue decouples producer and consumer, smoothing uneven traffic bursts

slides.notes: "Explain cache-aside with a product-page read example. Point to ElastiCache and SQS as the AWS services used. Exam hook: why does a queue decouple producer speed from consumer speed?"

slides.title: Absorbing Load Spikes

points.text: AWS: ElastiCache for caching, SQS for durable message queuing
Caching cuts repeated backend reads
While a queue lets producers continue without waiting for consumers

slides.notes: "Explain cache-aside with a product-page read example. Point to ElastiCache and SQS as the AWS services used. Exam hook: why does a queue decouple producer speed from consumer speed?"

slides.label: Analogy: supermarket
slides.title: Absorbing Load Spikes
slides.notes: TR analogy: A supermarket keeps frequently purchased items near the checkout for quick access (caching). During busy hours, customers wait in an orderly line instead of crowding the cashier (queuing). "Explain cache-aside with a product-page read example. Point to ElastiCache and SQS as the AWS services used. Exam hook: why does a queue decouple producer speed from consumer speed?"

slides.title: Handling Transient Failures
slides.lead: A momentary glitch should not fail a request outright. A timeout bounds how long to wait for a reply, and a retry resends the request

points.text: Exponential backoff: each retry waits longer, easing load on a struggling service
Jitter: randomizes the wait to stop retries arriving in sync
Retries need idempotent operations, such as calls with an idempotency key
Or repeats can duplicate effects
AWS SDKs apply backoff automatically on throttled or failed calls

slides.notes: "Idempotency is the real exam trap: a retried payment call can double-charge. AWS SDKs retry automatically with backoff built in."

slides.title: Stopping Cascading Failures
slides.lead: Retrying a service that is fully down wastes time and piles up requests; a circuit breaker stops calling it until it recovers

points.text: Closed state: requests flow normally, failures are counted
Open state: calls fail fast without reaching the service
Half-open state: a few test requests check if it recovered
Prevents one failing service from exhausting callers' threads and connections

slides.notes: "Name the three states clearly; half-open is the one learners forget. Service meshes or client libraries implement this pattern on AWS. Exam hook: what moves a breaker from half-open back to open?"

slides.label: Analogy: household electrical breaker
slides.title: Stopping Cascading Failures
slides.notes: TR analogy: A household electrical breaker trips and cuts power the moment it senses a fault, instead of letting wiring keep burning: just as the software pattern trips open and stops calls to a failing service. "Name the three states clearly; half-open is the one learners forget. Service meshes or client libraries implement this pattern on AWS. Exam hook: what moves a breaker from half-open back to open?"

slides.title: Reduced But Working
slides.lead: When a dependency fails or slows down, a system can return a simpler response instead of none, keeping the core function alive

points.text: Fallback response: cached or default data replaces a failed call
Feature shedding: non-critical features are disabled under heavy load
Partial results: showing some data beats showing an error page
Works together with circuit breakers, which trigger the fallback path

slides.notes: "Use an e-commerce example: a product page loads without the recommendations widget if that service is down. Exam hook: name one feature that is safe to shed under load."

slides.title: One Request, One Failure
slides.lead: Consider an API call to a checkout service that times out under load; tracing the path shows how each pattern responds in order

points.text: Request hits load balancer, forwarded to checkout service instance
Call exceeds the configured 3-second timeout and is abandoned
Client retries once after a 500ms backoff delay

slides.notes: "Walk the timeline left to right, pausing at the breaker-open step since that is the one students forget. Emphasise the fallback returns stale-but-useful data, not an error."

slides.title: One Request, One Failure

points.text: Second attempt also times out; further calls fail the same way and the failure count keeps rising
Breaker opens after 5 consecutive failures, blocking calls for 30 seconds
Fallback keeps the cart saved and shows a 'checkout busy, try again shortly' message
Instead of a raw error

slides.notes: "Walk the timeline left to right, pausing at the breaker-open step since that is the one students forget. Emphasise the fallback returns stale-but-useful data, not an error."

Quiz on Cloud-Native Applications. Q1. What does immutable infrastructure do instead of modifying running instances in place? Answer: It replaces them with newly built and tested instances. Q2. Swapping a local MySQL database for Amazon RDS needs what kind of change? Answer: Only a config change, not a code change. Q3. Why do companies split monoliths into microservices? Answer: Mainly to scale parts independently. Q4. Where does session data go so that any instance can serve any request? Answer: A shared cache such as Amazon ElastiCache. Q5. What does jitter add to retries? Answer: A random wait, so retries do not arrive in sync. Q6. What moves a circuit breaker from half-open back to open? Answer: The test requests fail again. Q7. Name one feature that is safe to shed under load. Answer: The recommendations widget.
